newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Lion Teck Chiang sees net up 70 pct 1997.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Lion Teck Chiang sees net up 70 pct 1997.

text.p: Property and steel group Lion Teck Chiang Ltd, part of Malaysian conglomerate The Lion Group, expects its net profit to soar nearly 70 percent this year, chief executive officer Sam Chong-Keen said on Monday.
Sam told Reuters the company, Singapore's second largest steel supplier, expected most of its future growth to come from its property developments in the city state and in Malaysia.
"With our large land banks and the growing Malaysian economy, I think the prospects are quite good," he said in an interview.
He said the company expected to make a net profit of Singapore $17.5 million in its year to June 30, 1997, up almost 70 percent from S$10.4 million last year.
Sam was speaking at the launch of his company's initial public offering (IPO) in Singapore in which it offered 32.52 million shares at S$1.30 each.
The IPO prospectus forecast a 1997 group turnover at S$151.8 million and a pre-tax profit of approximately S$24.9 million.
Sam said the group's property profits had exceeded those from steel operations for the first time last year.
Steel operations represented nearly 85 percent of the group's turnover of S$129.13 million last year but contributed just 29.4 percent of its S$13.75 million pre-tax profits.
Property development, with just 10.3 percent of turnover, made up 39.9 percent of pre-tax profits, the prospectus said.
"That will continue to be the trend with rising property prices," Sam said.

But he said the group was investing for the future in its steel sector, moving away from the import and sale of unfinished steel and towards secondary processing of steel rods ready for use in the construction industry.
"We are the second largest player in the steel market here in Singapore with 15-20 percent of the market, behind Natsteel , which has around 60 percent," he said.
"For steel, I think the market is looking increasingly competitive. The barriers to entry for just pure steel trading are low and the margins for those activities will be squeezed.

"So our strategy will be to move downsteam to the more value-added activities like cutting, bending of steel before delivery to construction sites. There the margins are much better and the barriers to entry are reasonably high," he said.
Sam said the steady stream of construction projects in Southeast Asia should ensure demand for its steel products.
"We are quite optimistic that construction growth will be fairly good," he said.

Lion Teck Chiang has property projects in Singapore and the southern Malaysian city of Johor Baru, and has also built up a large land bank in Malaysia with 1,500 acres (600 ha) of sites in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan.
"We see a great potential to develop this land, primarily for industrial use," he said.
Sam told the IPO news conference the company was also considering investing in property in Burma, but gave no details.
The IPO prospectus said the offer price of Singapore $1.30 represented a historical price-earnings ratio (PE) of 16.6 times and a forecast PE ratio of 10.0 times.
The offer will close on April 15 and trading is expected to begin on a when-ready basis on April 17.
